Title: East of Eden
Author: John Steinbeck
My Review:
If theres someone who actually reinvented the wheel, but in a much better way, its Steinbeck! He mixed the oldest stories, added that one perfect word, and said: Here. Read it. Decide what you’re going to do with it.

John Steinbeck didn’t just write East of Eden—he handed you a loaded gun disguised as a book. And the bullet? One Hebrew word: timshel. “Thou mayest.” That’s it! That single word, dropped early and quietly, explodes everything you thought you knew about good, evil, fate, and choice.

The whole story is built on the Bible’s oldest family dramas—Adam and Eve in the Garden, Cain and Abel in the field. Steinbeck grabbed both of them, mashed them together, and sprinkled in that pinch of salt: timshel. Suddenly the old stories aren’t locked in stone anymore. They’re alive, messy, and waiting for you to decide what happens next.

And here’s the genius: there is no big, thunderous revelation at the end. No “aha!” twist that makes you gasp and flip back to page one. The meaning is right there in the beginning, whispered early: thou mayest. You already know the choice is yours. Just like in Dostoevsky’s Crime and Punishment, where the title tells you the crime will happen and the punishment will follow—yet you can’t stop reading because the real story is how the soul wrestles inside the inevitability. That’s why these books are timeless. That’s what makes them a classic. They don’t hide the ending; they show you that journey is everything.

The first quarter of East of Eden is slow. Steinbeck builds the valley, the families, the quiet resentments, the land itself. You wonder: Is anything even going to happen? Then the second three-quarters hit like a freight train. Once the brothers grow, once the sins start repeating, once timshel lands like a quiet bomb—you’re gone. I slogged through the first half over weeks. The second half? I devoured it in one breathless stretch. Couldn’t put it down. The pages turned themselves.

Because timshel isn’t just a word—it’s power handed back to you. It says evil isn’t destiny. Sin isn’t a curse you inherit forever. You mayest overcome it. You mayest choose differently. You mayest rule over it.

And when that sinks in, something shifts inside. You feel taller. Stronger. Suddenly the weight of your own choices doesn’t crush you—it frees you.

So read it. Feel the slow burn, survive the hook, and let timshel change the way you look at your own life.

This book stays with you forever.

Title: Sweet Thursday (Cannery Row, #2)
Author: John Steinbeck
My Review:
Picking up right where Cannery Row left off back in ‘45! We’re back in that misty, sardine-scented slice of Monterey after World War II, with the canneries still churning but the vibe a little heavier—like everyone’s got a quiet hangover from the fighting. The first book was pure, goofy escapism with folks just drifting through their days; this one feels more like catching up with those same pals over coffee, swapping laughs for a few “what ifs” and a touch of grown-up ache.

You slide right back in with the crew: Doc, the deep-thinking lab guy who’s a bit more blue-eyed and war-worn this time; Mack and his Flophouse buddies, still masterminding plans that crash and burn in the funniest ways; Hazel, bless him, dropping those earnest, off-the-wall thoughts that had me chuckling out loud; and Suzy, the new girl from the Bear Flag who brings some fresh spark (and awkward romance) to the mix.

Steinbeck still keeps it loose—no big plot twists, just those quick, breezy chapters that feel like flipping through old photos. The gang’s big mission? Cheer up Doc with matchmaking gone wrong, frog hunts that turn into comedy sketches, and parties that start with big dreams and end in glorious, sloppy messes.

It’s got that Steinbeck magic: the humor’s sharp and warm (Hazel’s bits are highlights), and underneath, there’s real heart about picking yourself up after life’s kicked you, leaning on friends through the rough patches, and squeezing joy out of the everyday—like nursing a beer at Lee’s while the ocean hums.

Compared to Cannery Row, it’s less wide-open innocent, more settled-in and reflective, which I loved. Overall, a solid 3.5 stars—charming and comforting, but not quite the knockout its predecessor was. If Cannery Row hooked you, this is a must for the full friendship arc.

My next up? Definitely Easy of Eden!

Title: The Pearl
Author: John Steinbeck
My Review:
John Steinbeck wrote The Pearl in 1947. It’s a quick book, like a smooth rock from the beach, fits in your hand, but hits hard when you think about it. Set in a sunny, dusty Mexican village where people dive for pearls to survive, it feels like an old folktale, easy to follow but with a real bite. The whole thing sticks to one family and how one big find changes everything, for better and worse.

You meet Kino, a calm diver, his smart wife Juana, and their baby Coyotito. They live simple, singing to the sea like it’s a friend. Then a giant pearl turns up, and suddenly they’re dreaming big: school for the kid, a better house, standing up to the town bosses who’ve pushed them around. But talk spreads quick, and greedy folks show up, dealers cheating on prices, a doctor who ignores them till money’s in sight, even the priest sniffing around. Steinbeck sums it all up in just a few chapters that flow like water, starting hopeful and turning rough, showing how that pearl tests love and trust.

The real stuff sneaks in: how chasing more can ruin you, how the rich keep the poor stuck with fake smiles, and how family love makes you fight hard, even if it hurts. Steinbeck keeps the words pretty but plain, like sea air mixed with sweat. After the fun Cannery Row series, this is a sharp wake-up, raw and quick, makes you pause.

I’d give it 3.5 stars as it grabs you with its punch and heart, but the story’s lesson feels a little too clear-cut now and then. It’s a fast read that stays with you; good for a quiet day.

Title: Of Mice and Men
Author: John Steinbeck
My Review:
I won’t give spoilers :)

I thought of reading one author at a time, every single book or at-least their best seven, just to get them completely. And I decided to start John Steinbeck.

A short and simple but terrifyingly dark novella that showed men divided into the two roles of prey and predator. How friendship is tested in the world full of these roles, couldn’t be more beautifully explained.

Two lifelong friends but completely opposite men, George (short, smart and always looks after Lennie) and Lennie (big and astonishingly dumb guy with a dream of taming and feeding soft furry rabbits) who move across the country with a simple dream in their mind, “living off the fatta the lan”!

The dream. That ‘fatta lan!’ — a patch of green where you plant your own crops, raise your own rabbits, and finally call something yours. It’s the American Dream shrunk down to size for two broke nobodies, and Steinbeck makes you believe in it for a heartbeat.

Then he reminds you: dreams are for dreamers, and this world’s for hustlers. But that’s the beauty — he leaves you wrestling with the “what ifs” long after the last page. The weight of doing right by someone who can’t do right by themselves… it’s all buried in this very short book.

Man plans, God Laughs

A proverb that means life is unpredictable and that even the most carefully laid plans can be disrupted by unexpected events. Thats what happens!

This is surely one of the best books for getting into reading John Steinbeck and definitely the best for getting into the American literature. Solid 8.5/10

Quick question! Suppose you had a dog who was with you ever since he was a puppy. He has spent his whole life with you but now he’s old and can’t see, can’t walk can’t do the least of things to survive… would you shoot him and free him of his misery of would you keep him alive and let him suffer till death just because?

This was my first Steinbeck!

Title: Cannery Row (Cannery Row, #1)
Author: John Steinbeck
My Review:
Even when researching Steinbeck’s writings, the most renowned books that I came across were East of Eden, Grapes of Wrath, Of Mice and Men, which got me thinking that Steinbeck’s writings are deeper to a level where humour can’t reach but man oh man… Cannery Row!

Cannery Row in Monterey in California is a poem, a stink, a grating noise, a quality of light, a tone, a habit, a nostalgia, a dream. Cannery Row is the gathered and scattered, tin and iron and rust and splintered wood, chipped pavement and weedy lots and junk heaps, sardine canneries of corrugated iron, honky tonks, restaurants and whore houses, and little crowded groceries, and laboratories and flophouses. Its inhabitant are, as the man once said, “whores, pimps, gambler and sons of bitches,” by which he meant Everybody. Had the man looked through another peephole he might have said, “Saints and angels and martyrs and holy men” and he would have meant the same thing.

The picture you get in mind after reading this paragraph is exactly what Cannery Row is!

While not having one strong plot, this book contains short interconnected narratives of the quirky yet utterly memorable people of Cannery Row in Monterey where the business seemed to bloom while Canneries packed cans of sardines and tuna. It’s less of a plot line and more of an characterisation of the people in the story. While being completely unaware of the context of canneries, this book will simply get you to travel back in time to the early 1900’s and see the tough and innocent lives of people living there.

The book revolves around Doc’, the marine biologist and own a laboratory, who’s the nicest to the people living there whom he’s helped in some way or another. Mack, the layabout misfit and the leader of his troupe of good natured boys. Dora, who runs a brothel. Lee Chong a short Chinese grocer and many many more. The people and the way they’re explained is just amazing. All the characters, in their own way want to do something good for the Doc but the trouble is, it just goes the other way! And the fact that the simplest of things are so intensely defined is amazing! Every single chapter is intensely character driven. These folks are so disarmingly innocent that humor bubbles up from every awkward exchange and half-baked idea. Get to know them, and they’ll pull you right into their world, making you wonder how it would feel to swap your daily routine for their salty, sun-bleached days.

While every chapter not being more than 3 pages, you’ll genuinely feel like you’re reading a sitcom. This, being my second book going through Steinbeck’s, I just can’t wait to read more.

Here are a few quotes that just stick.

“Where men hungering for love, destroy everything lovable about them.”

“It has always seemed strange to me...The things we admire in men, kindness and generosity, openness, honesty, understanding and feeling, are the concomitants of failure in our system. And those traits we detest, sharpness, greed, acquisitiveness, meanness, egotism and self-interest, are the traits of success. And while men admire the quality of the first they love the produce of the second.”

“It’s all fine to say, “Time will heal everything, this too shall pass away. People will forget”—and things like that when you are not involved, but when you are there is no passage of time, people do not forget and you are in the middle of something that does not change.”

“For there are two possible reactions to social ostracism - either a man emerges determined to be better, purer, and kindlier or he goes bad, challenges the world and does even worse things. The last is by far the commonest reaction to stigma.”

And a few funny ones :) Trust me, there are so many.
